summary:
Ondo State stands under Nigeria's national framework. Same-sex sexual activity has been illegal across the country since 1916, and the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act, passed by the House of Representatives on 30 May 2013 and signed into law by President Goodluck Jonathan in January 2014, criminalises all forms of same-sex unions with up to 14 years' imprisonment.

The death-penalty layer does not reach Ondo. The twelve states operating Shari'a-based criminal codes, where male sodomy can be punished by death including by stoning, sit in the northern part of the country; Ondo, a southern state, stands under the secular national framework, whose maximum penalty in the southern portion of the country is a life sentence.

The UK Home Office's June 2025 country policy and information note records countrywide harm patterns of arrests, detention and mob violence against LGBT+ people, patterns that apply in Ondo as in the rest of the country. The note also quotes Section 217 of the Criminal Code, under which any male committing or procuring an act of gross indecency with another male, in public or private, is guilty of a felony liable to three years' imprisonment; this gross-indecency offence applies in southern states such as Ondo.

Victor Oluwasina Ayeni, a senior lecturer in law at Adekunle Ajasin University in Ondo state, observed in a January 2017 book chapter that the Code fails to define what constitutes an act of gross indecency, leaving the offence's scope open to interpretation.

No state-specific protective statute or enforcement divergence is documented for Ondo: the state recognises no legal gender identity, provides no anti-discrimination protections and recognises no same-sex relationships.
tangentialFactors:
Nationwide, trans people face lethal violence with official misgendering and subsequent impunity: the beaten body of the Abuja trans TikToker 'Abuja Area Mama', a 33-year-old transgender woman, was found on the Katampe-Mabushi expressway in Abuja on 9 August 2024, hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; police opened a 'thorough and discreet' investigation, and no suspects had been charged six months later.

Wikipedia's Nigeria overview records that mass arrests of LGBTQ+ Nigerians are common, especially in northern states, and that same-sex conduct has been criminalised since 1916.

outOfScopeNotes:
Ondo is not named in the Wikipedia Nigeria LGBT-rights page, so the state-level characterisation rests on its status as a southern state under the secular national framework rather than on state-specific documentation.

No Ondo-specific enforcement incidents, arrests or state legislative proposals are recorded in the source inventory; whether state practice diverges from the national pattern is unresolved.
